newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BA ground staff open door to peace talks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BA ground staff open door to peace talks.

text.p: British Airways' ground staff voted for strike action on Monday but also held out an olive branch of peace talks with the airliner.

But as BA attempts to save 1.0 billion pounds ($1.7 billion) by 2000 in cost-cuts, a deadlock continued over a parallel dispute with its cabin crew, which has sparked a bitter five-month row over pay and conditions.

BA's chief executive Robert Ayling said that Bill Morris, general secretary of the Transport and General (T&G) Workers' union had written to BA suggesting peace talks with ground staff over the planned sale of its catering unit.
Ayling welcomed T&G's peace move and said he was ready to start discussions immediately.
"Talks will happen as far as I'm concerned, and my managers are ready now. I can't see why we can't have an agreement very quickly," he told a news conference.
Earlier, the T&G said of the 69 percent of BA's ground staff who returned votes, 62.5 percent had voted in favour of a strike.
Monday's vote for strike action by ground staff increases the likelihood of disruption to flights after cabin crew last week also voted overwhelmingly for industrial action.
News of Monday's ballot pulled down BA's share price, which closed 11 pence lower at 684 1/2p as analysts warned the cost of confrontation would be heavy if passengers defected to rival airlines.
Analysts said the impact on BA profits could be heavy, especially if passengers decided to start switching airlines.
"A strike would make a massive difference to BA -- financially in the short term as well as hurting it long-term," said Chris Avery, analyst at Paribas.
Industry observers pointed out that when BA faced the threat of a pilots' strike last year, which failed to materialise, the cost to profits was far from negligible.
"That dispute cost them more than 10 million pounds" even though no action took place, another transport analyst said.
Although Ayling said BA was banking on a swift agreement with ground staff, he continued to take a harder line over the separate dispute with cabin crew.
He said five months of talks had failed to yield an agreement and he would not reopen talks until the BASSA trade union, affiliated to the T&G, put its "militancy" behind it.
He said the situation with the ground staff was different because no negotiations had taken place so far over the disputed plan to sell BA's catering business.
Ayling, who cancelled his trip to witness Britain's handover of Hong Kong to China in order to take on the unions, described Morris' invitation as "a welcome sign".
"We are pleased it has happened, it is a good development and is good for customers," he said.

Meanwhile, T&G's national secretary for aviation, George Ryde, told reporters there was a meeting scheduled later on Monday with BA's cabin crew staff to discuss whether they would go ahead with a strike.
BA has drawn up a battle-plan to keep services flying.

All management have been re-trained to allow them to take on more roles, extra security will be brought in to get strike breakers through picket-lines and the group is also willing to hire external staff to take on BA strikers' jobs.

The airline, fresh from a 60 million pound facelift and in the midst of seeking regulatory clearance for its alliance with AMR's American Airlines, has placed all operations on red alert to combat the threat. ($ = 0.601 British Pounds)
